title: External Ventricular Drainage: A Practical Guide for Neuro-Anesthesiologists
condition_or_topic: Management of external ventricular drainage (EVD) in neurocritical care
clinical_background: EVD can provide urgent cerebrospinal fluid diversion for acute hydrocephalus and can also be used to monitor intracranial pressure. Placement carries risks, including infection, hemorrhage, catheter obstruction, and malposition. Despite its frequent use, practices vary, particularly in drainage and weaning strategies. Cerebrospinal fluid drainage in severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains debated; evidence concerning external lumbar drainage (ELD) is more limited, partly because of concerns about cerebral herniation.
objectives: Review the relevant literature and present a practical guide to EVD management based on recent recommendations.

Examine indications, timing, management, and complications of EVD in neurocritical care, with particular attention to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).
study_design: Literature review of relevant articles published from 2010 to 2022, identified through PubMed/MEDLINE using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). The search placed no restrictions on article language.

population.description: The review focused on neurocritical care patients requiring EVD, particularly those with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), or intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH).
inclusion_criteria: Relevant articles from 2010 to 2022 addressing the indications, timing, management, or complications of EVD in neurocritical care

interventions: Rapid wean approach (RWA) and gradual wean approach (GWA)
External lumbar drainage (ELD) for cerebrospinal fluid diversion
comparators: Rapid wean approach (RWA) versus gradual wean approach (GWA)
External lumbar drainage (ELD) versus external ventricular drainage (EVD)
main_conclusion: EVD can be lifesaving in acute hydrocephalus, but its management remains uncertain across clinical settings. The authors conclude that intermittent drainage in SAH carries more complications, that VPS dependency may be greater with RWA than with GWA, and that continuous drainage is customary in TBI despite insufficient evidence favoring either approach. ELD may help control ICP, but its safety evidence is inadequate for firm recommendations.
narrative_summary: This review examined EVD indications, timing, management, and complications in neurocritical care, with particular attention to SAH, severe TBI, and IVH. A PubMed/MEDLINE search covering relevant articles from 2010 to 2022 yielded 53 selected articles; pediatric cases were excluded. In SAH, an cited randomized trial reported more catheter obstruction, replacement, and hemorrhage with intermittent than with continuous drainage, without a significant difference in vasospasm. Findings on weaning were inconsistent: a cited observational study found fewer shunts at 90 days with RWA (VPS-free: 83% in RWA vs. 69% in GWA, HR: 0.52, p = 0.041), whereas a cited randomized study reported more VPS placement with RWA (93.9% vs. 61.2%). A cited meta-analysis found no difference in VPS dependency (RR = 1.24, 95% CI: 0.99–1.55, I-squared = 34.6%). For severe TBI, continuous drainage is commonly used, but the review identifies insufficient high-quality evidence to establish the better drainage strategy. In IH/IVH, EVD reduces ICP, while a reduction in morbidity or mortality has not been established by statistically significant data; the clinical benefits of intraventricular thrombolysis remain under investigation. EVD complications include obstruction, hemorrhage, misplacement, and infection. ELD appears capable of reducing ICP when medical treatment fails, including when EVD has failed, but available safety data cannot support conclusive recommendations. The authors call for further studies to clarify EVD management and ELD safety.
interpretation: The authors regard EVD as potentially life-saving in acute hydrocephalus, while emphasizing that its optimal management varies by clinical setting and remains unsettled. In SAH, intermittent drainage carries a greater complication burden, including catheter obstruction, hemorrhage, and replacement. Evidence on weaning is inconsistent: the authors' conclusion suggests greater VPS dependence with RWA than with GWA, whereas the studies discussed report conflicting findings. For severe TBI, continuous drainage is customary despite insufficient evidence favoring either drainage strategy. In IH/IVH, EVD lowers ICP, but a statistically significant reduction in morbidity or mortality has not been established. Intraventricular thrombolytic therapy remains under investigation. ELD appears capable of controlling ICP when medical treatment fails, but its safety and its efficacy relative to EVD cannot yet be established conclusively.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The cited trial by Olson et al. found more complications with intermittent than continuous drainage in SAH, without a significant difference in vasospasm. Evidence on weaning conflicts: Klopfenstein et al. found similar VPS placement rates with RWA and GWA but a shorter hospital stay with RWA; a multicenter observational study associated RWA with a lower VPS rate at 90 days; a German study associated RWA with earlier and more frequent VPS placement; and a meta-analysis found a shorter hospital stay with RWA but no difference in VPS dependence. For EVD placement, cited comparisons of operating-room and bedside procedures reported differing patterns of infection, bleeding, and placement accuracy. Studies cited for ELD reported reductions in ICP and favorable effects on CPP or the need for other ICP-lowering treatments, while the reviewed safety evidence remained insufficient for firm conclusions.
clinical_implications: Excessive lowering of ICP during CSF drainage in SAH may increase the risk of renewed aneurysmal bleeding.
In severe TBI, EVD can serve both to monitor ICP and to divert CSF when ICP is elevated.
In IH/IVH, the demonstrated reduction in ICP should not be taken as evidence of a statistically significant improvement in morbidity or mortality.
ELD may provide ICP control in selected patients, including when EVD has failed, but the available evidence does not establish its comparative efficacy or safety against EVD.
Catheter obstruction can precipitate acute hydrocephalus; infection may progress to ventriculitis or cerebritis.
practice_implications: The operating room is generally accepted as the preferred setting for EVD placement, although emergency circumstances may require another setting.
For SAH, most authors favor limiting CSF drainage in accordance with hydrocephalus severity and ICP, keeping the drainage system high or closed to avoid excessive ICP reduction.

For intermittent drainage in ICU patients, CSF release is suggested when ICP > 20 mm Hg persists for more than 5 min, with clamping once ICP returns to normal. In awake patients who can be assessed neurologically, headache, nausea or vomiting, and CSF leakage from the wound are indications to open the drain.
With continuous drainage, the physician determines the volume released and adjusts drainage according to neuroimaging, the underlying condition, and ICP monitoring.
For severe TBI, the Brain Trauma Foundation recommends continuous rather than intermittent EVD drainage (Level III), while the authors note that high-quality comparative evidence is lacking.

In IH/IVH, EVD placement is required when medical treatment does not adequately lower ICP and clinical deterioration occurs; placing it early in patients with good neurological status remains controversial.
Catheter blockage requires prompt replacement to prevent acute hydrocephalus.

A metal needle may be an acceptable alternative when neither ICP monitoring nor ventricular hemorrhage is present. The authors report that antibiotic-impregnated and antimicrobial-coated catheters are used similarly, with a slight preference for silver-coated EVD.
The authors do not make a conclusive recommendation for ELD to control ICP after TBI because safety evidence remains insufficient.
limitations: The literature does not provide high-quality evidence to favor intermittent or continuous EVD drainage in severe TBI, and the authors found no studies specifically examining optimal EVD management in this population.
Scientific evidence on EVD management in severe TBI and IH/IVH is more limited than that available for SAH.
No randomized clinical trials were available for the intraventricular fibrinolytic treatment discussed in IH/IVH, and its effect on clinical outcomes remains under investigation.
The available evidence cannot support firm conclusions about ELD safety in TBI or establish its efficacy and safety relative to EVD.
open_questions: Which EVD drainage and weaning strategies are preferable in each clinical setting?
Does intraventricular thrombolytic therapy improve clinical outcomes in IH/IVH?
What are the safety profile and comparative efficacy of ELD versus EVD for ICP control after TBI?
future_directions: Conduct further randomized clinical trials to clarify EVD management across clinical situations.
Complete studies assessing the clinical outcomes of intraventricular thrombolytic therapy in IH/IVH.
Undertake larger prospective observational studies of ELD safety, potentially followed by randomized controlled studies assessing whether its therapeutic performance is comparable to EVD.

drugs_and_therapies.name: external ventricular drainage (EVD)

drugs_and_therapies.name: external lumbar drainage (ELD)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Diverts CSF through a lumbar drain without passing a drain through cerebral parenchyma.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Discussed as a potential option for ICP control after TBI, although its safety evidence is insufficient for firm recommendations.

drugs_and_therapies.name: intermittent EVD drainage
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Keeps the drain closed except when symptoms or increased ICP prompt CSF release.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Compared with continuous drainage, particularly after SAH; a cited randomized trial reported more complications with the intermittent approach.

drugs_and_therapies.name: continuous EVD drainage
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Leaves the drain open for ongoing CSF release.

drugs_and_therapies.name: rapid wean approach (RWA)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Immediately closes the drain; the proposed effect is recruitment of CSF resorption pathways after pressure rises.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An EVD discontinuation strategy compared with GWA for VPS dependency and hospital stay after SAH.

drugs_and_therapies.name: gradual wean approach (GWA)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Progressively raises the open drain before clamping it; the proposed effect is gradual rebalancing of CSF production and reabsorption.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An EVD discontinuation strategy compared with RWA after SAH.

notable_adverse_events: EVD obstruction may require prompt replacement to prevent acute hydrocephalus; the review associates more drain failure with continuous drainage and reports RR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.27–0.74, I-squared = 0%, without specifying the RR's reference category.

Hemorrhage and catheter misplacement after EVD have a reported incidence of up to 12%; oral anticoagulants or antiplatelet therapy are identified as factors affecting hemorrhagic complications, while brain edema and midline shift are identified as principal misplacement risk factors.
EVD-related infection, which can progress to ventriculitis or cerebritis, has a reported incidence ranging from 0 to 27%; the review relates infection primarily to EVD duration.
In Olson et al.'s randomized trial, intermittent rather than continuous drainage had more catheter clogging, EVD replacement, and hemorrhage; no rates are supplied.
In Altschul et al.'s analysis, infection occurred in 13% for ER EVD compared with 7.7% for ICU/OR EVD (p = 0.03).
A cited systematic review reported iatrogenic bleeding of 18.16% with ICU EVD versus 17.50% with OR EVD, and ventriculostomy-related infection of 7.28% with ICU EVD versus 8.06% with OR EVD.

A cited 2015 meta-analysis reported an overall EVD infection incidence of 10.6/1000 catheterdays, approximately 19.6/1000 catheter-days for EVD in place for less than 7 days, and 8/1000 catheter-days for more than 10 days.
A prospective UK and Ireland cohort reported a 9.3% EVD infection rate at 30 days after placement.

In the ELD evidence discussed, a single case involved pupillary changes and cerebral herniation requiring urgent surgery, with good neurological recovery; the review states that no included study reported ELD use directly contributing to mortality.

Infections occurred at a rate of 3.9% in the studies included in the ELD safety discussion, although some affected patients had both EVD and ELD; separately cited literature reports 4.2–7% for ELD and 7-9% for EVD.

subgroup_analyses: For patients with SAH, the cited comparisons of intermittent and continuous drainage found no significant difference in vasospasm, VPS dependency, or hospital stay; Olson et al. reported more catheter-related complications and hemorrhage with intermittent drainage.

For patients with SAH undergoing EVD weaning, the cited studies differed: Klopfenstein et al. found no significant VPS-rate difference, a multicenter cohort associated RWA with lower VPS placement at 90 days, and a German randomized study reported more and earlier VPS placement with RWA. The cited meta-analysis found no VPS-dependency difference.

For patients with TBI, a cited prospective observational study reported fewer refractory ICP episodes (p > 0.001) and better survival (p = 0.006) with intermittent EVD drainage; the article states that high-quality comparative evidence on drainage strategies is lacking.

For patients with IH/IVH, the article reports ICP reduction with EVD but no statistically significant evidence of reduced morbidity or mortality; the clinical-outcome benefit of intraventricular thrombolytics remained under investigation.

By placement location, Schodel et al. found fewer infections and catheter-trajectory hemorrhages with ICU BKS placement than with OR mechanical drilling, whereas Altschul et al. reported more infection after ER placement than after ICU/OR placement. A separate systematic review reported the location-specific accuracy, bleeding, and infection rates in main_findings.
By duration of EVD placement, a cited meta-analysis reported infection incidence of approximately 19.6/1000 catheter-days for less than 7 days and 8/1000 catheter-days for more than 10 days.
secondary_results: In the SAH drainage discussion, the review describes continuous drainage as theoretically allowing better CSF clearance and possibly less vasospasm, but with a greater risk of ventricular collapse; it does not present this theoretical benefit as a demonstrated reduction in vasospasm.
The review states that rapid and gradual weaning are distinct from the choice between continuous and intermittent drainage, even though the approaches may be used together.

For severe TBI, the article reports that the Brain Trauma Foundation recommended continuous over intermittent EVD drainage (Level III), while noting a lack of high-quality evidence favoring either drainage strategy.

The review describes the benefits of intraventricular thrombolytic therapy on clinical outcomes in IH/IVH as unresolved; it identifies CLEAR III Clot Lysis: Evaluating Accelerated Resolution of Intraventricular Hemorrhage Phase III as ongoing.

For ELD after TBI, the article describes encouraging evidence of ICP control when medical management has failed, including where EVD has failed, but considers the safety evidence insufficient for conclusive recommendations and states that its comparative efficacy and safety versus EVD are unknown.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: External ventricular drainage (EVD) can be lifesaving in acute hydrocephalus, but its optimal management remains uncertain. This review examines evidence on EVD indications, timing, management, and complications in neurocritical care, particularly in subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). In SAH, intermittent drainage is associated with more complications, including catheter obstruction, bleeding, and replacement. The abstract suggests greater ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependency after rapid rather than gradual weaning. In TBI, continuous drainage is conventionally used despite a lack of evidence favoring either drainage strategy. Evidence concerning severe TBI and intraparenchymal/intraventricular hemorrhage is more limited. EVD is necessary in several clinical settings, while further randomized trials are needed to establish how best to manage it.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: EVD is among the most frequently performed neurosurgical procedures. Claude Nicholas Le Cat first described it in 1744. It may save lives in acute hydrocephalus arising from various conditions or in elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). A computerized transduction system permits continuous ICP monitoring, although EVD has a higher complication risk than intraparenchymal monitoring devices. Temporary outward diversion of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) during brain infection is another possible indication. Despite the procedure's relative speed and simplicity, complications include meningitis, ventriculitis, bleeding along the catheter path, and catheter malposition or obstruction. Management of moderate and severe TBI seeks to limit secondary injury by avoiding raised ICP and maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), with treatment intensity escalated until ICP is controlled under protocols based on Brain Trauma Foundation (BTF) guidelines. Initial treatments for intracranial hypertension include sedation, mild hypocapnia, and hyperosmolar therapy; refractory cases may warrant consideration of CSF diversion, barbiturate coma, or decompressive craniectomy. Technical practice and EVD management vary substantially, including placement technique and location, postoperative complications, catheter impregnation, drainage, and weaning. CSF drainage in severe TBI remains disputed. EVD has been studied more extensively than external lumbar drainage (ELD) for lowering ICP. Concern about transtentorial or tonsillar herniation historically made controlled lumbar drainage seem contraindicated in raised ICP, although studies over recent decades suggest possible use in carefully selected patients. ELD is absent from current BTF guidelines because supporting evidence is poor. The article aims to review the literature and provide practical EVD management guidance based on recent recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE, accessed on 1 November 2022, using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms: “External Ventricular Drain”, “Intracranial Pressure”, “ICP Monitoring”, “Subarachnoid Hemorrhage”, “Intraventricular Hemorrhage”, “External lumbar drainage”, “Cerebral Herniation”, “Traumatic Brain Injury”, “Non-invasive ICP Monitoring”, and “Acute Hydrocephalus”. They considered relevant recent articles from 2010 to 2022 concerning EVD indications, timing, management, and complications in neurocritical care, particularly for SAH, severe TBI, and IVH. Pediatric cases were excluded, with no language restriction. The selection comprised 53 articles.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Overview
document_sections.content: Acute hydrocephalus is the principal indication for EVD and can follow SAH, intraparenchymal hemorrhage with or without ventricular extension, infection, brain tumors, or shunt failure. Brain Trauma Foundation guidance also includes EVD for treatment and ICP monitoring in severe TBI. Emergency placement occurs in operating rooms (ORs), emergency rooms (ERs), and intensive care units (ICUs). Studies, many retrospective, have compared complications across settings. In Schodel et al.'s 312 cases, placement with a Bolt Kit System (BKS) in the ICU had significantly lower postprocedural CSF infection and catheter-tract bleeding rates than conventional mechanical drilling in the OR (p = 0.032 and p = 0.018, respectively). Altschul et al.'s retrospective study of 710 patients reported infection in 13% after ER placement versus 7.7% after ICU/OR placement (p = 0.03). A systematic review reported better placement accuracy by Kakarla grading score in the OR than the ICU (84.25% vs. 68.29%), slightly more iatrogenic bleeding in the ICU than the OR (18.16% vs. 17.50%), and slightly fewer ventriculostomy-related infections in the ICU than the OR (7.28% vs. 8.06%). Its findings suggest that setting choice may benefit different patient populations differently. The authors note that one-shot antibiotic prophylaxis is consistently given for OR placement but not always for ICU placement, and describe a lower infection risk with OR placement on that basis. Most neurosurgical units use the OR, although the ICU and, exceptionally, a general ward have also been reported. Placement outside the OR has been linked to more postoperative infections; the OR is therefore generally accepted as the preferred setting. Catheter options include smaller metal needles (1.2 mm), which need a smaller skin incision, and larger polyurethane catheters (3 mm), which incorporate a tip sensor for ICP monitoring. Polyurethane EVD is routinely used in most hospitals, especially for IVH or TBI. A metal needle may suffice when ICP monitoring is unnecessary and ventricular bleeding is absent. Catheters may be impregnated with clindamycin, rifampicin, or gentamycin, or coated with silver or hydrogel. Compared with uncoated EVD, both types have been associated with fewer postoperative infections, without a significant difference between impregnated and coated catheters. Their use is similar, with a slight preference for silver-coated EVD.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. EVD in Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
document_sections.content: SAH is a cerebrovascular condition with substantial potential for morbidity and mortality. A conspicuous proportion of affected patients develop acute obstructive hydrocephalus treated by EVD. Most authors favor limiting CSF drainage, while accounting for hydrocephalus severity and ICP, by setting the system high or keeping it closed. This approach reflects historical evidence that excessive ICP reduction raises the risk of aneurysmal re-breakage.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1. Intermittent vs. Continuous Drainage
document_sections.content: Continuous and intermittent drainage are the principal accepted CSF drainage approaches. With intermittent drainage, EVD stays closed until symptoms develop or ICP rises. For ICU patients, CSF release is suggested when ICP > 20 mm Hg persists for more than 5 min; the drain is clamped once ICP normalizes. In awake patients who can undergo neurological assessment, symptoms guide drainage: headache, nausea or vomiting, and CSF leakage from the wound indicate opening the EVD. Intermittent drainage requires continuous monitoring but was not described as creating further clinical concerns. With continuous drainage, the system remains open, raising questions about drainage volume, weaning timing and method, and the need for intermittent ICP monitoring. The physician determines the volume released. A conventional setting is 10 mL/h, targeting approximately 100–300 mL per day; subsequent adjustments depend on neuroimaging, the underlying condition, and ICP. In SAH, continuous drainage might theoretically clear CSF more effectively and reduce vasospasm, but it also poses greater risk of ventricular collapse. Comparisons have not shown significant differences between continuous and intermittent approaches in vasospasm, ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS) dependency, or hospital length of stay. In a randomized trial, Olson et al. found more catheter obstruction, EVD replacement, and hemorrhage with intermittent than continuous drainage, without a significant difference in vasospasm risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2. Rapid vs. Gradual Weaning Strategy
document_sections.content: Rapid and gradual EVD weaning are separate choices from drainage strategy, even though continuous drainage is associated with rapid weaning and intermittent drainage with gradual weaning. The rapid wean approach (RWA) closes the system immediately at a time judged favorable from clinical findings and neuroimaging. Drainage stops, while the catheter remains available for monitoring; symptomatic hydrocephalus can then be identified and treated promptly. Its proposed mechanism is recruitment of CSF reabsorption through arachnoid granulations after a rapid pressure rise, potentially enabling earlier successful EVD discontinuation. The gradual wean approach (GWA) keeps the drain open while raising it over several days. Usually, after the system is raised above 25 cm H2O, it is clamped and discontinued. Its proposed mechanism is progressive adjustment of CSF production and reabsorption over 2–3 days. Findings across comparisons differ. Klopfenstein et al. studied 81 patients with aneurysmal SAH in 2004 and found no significant association between weaning approach and VPS placement (63.4% in RWA vs. 62.5% in GWA; p = 0.932). RWA was associated with a shorter hospital stay (mean days: 15.8 days in GWA vs. 12.7 days in RWA, p < 0.001). A multicenter observational cohort of 185 patients with aneurysmal SAH requiring EVD associated RWA with a lower VPS rate at 90 days (VPS-free: 83% in RWA vs. 69% in GWA, HR: 0.52, p = 0.041). More weaning attempts were associated with greater likelihood of VPS (95% CI: 1.8–4.8, OR = 2.9, p < 0.0001), while hospital length of stay did not differ significantly between strategies. A German study in 2018 randomized 965 patients with SAH and EVD and found VPS placement to be more frequent and earlier with RWA than GWA (93.9% vs. 61.2%, respectively); RWA was independently associated with shunt dependency (p = 0.026). A recent meta-analysis associated RWA with shorter hospitalization (SMD = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.22–0.47, I-squared = 0%) but found no difference in VPS dependency (RR = 1.24, 95% CI: 0.99–1.55, I-squared = 34.6%). Another systematic review and meta-analysis of weaning strategies is ongoing.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. EVD in Severe TBI
document_sections.content: In TBI, EVD both monitors ICP and diverts CSF when ICP is elevated. The authors found no studies directly examining appropriate EVD management in TBI. A recent prospective observational comparison of intraparenchymal and EVD ICP monitoring used intermittent drainage and reported therapeutic benefit, with fewer refractory ICP episodes (p > 0.001) and better survival (p = 0.006). The Brain Trauma Foundation recognizes therapeutic and monitoring roles for EVD in severe TBI and recommends continuous over intermittent drainage (Level III). Nevertheless, high-quality evidence supporting either drainage approach is lacking, and continuous CSF drainage is the most common practice worldwide.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. EVD in Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage with Intraventricular Involvement
document_sections.content: Intraparenchymal/intraventricular hemorrhage (IH/IVH) can obstruct CSF flow and cause acute obstructive hydrocephalus. EVD is required when medical treatment does not adequately lower ICP and the patient deteriorates clinically. Early placement in neurologically well patients with IH/IVH remains controversial. EVD lowers ICP in IH/IVH, but statistically significant evidence of reduced morbidity or mortality is unavailable. Although randomized trials are lacking, observational studies describe better outcomes with intraventricular fibrinolysis in some patients with associated SAH and IH/IVH. A recent phase II study examined intraventricular thrombolytic safety in massive ventricular bleeding: recombinant plasminogen factor (rt-PA) at 1 mg every 8 h provided good liquor clearance without an elevated bleeding risk. A phase III evaluation of clinical outcomes, CLEAR III Clot Lysis: Evaluating Accelerated Resolution of Intraventricular Hemorrhage Phase III, is ongoing.

document_sections.heading: 3.5. Surgical Technique
document_sections.content: Several EVD entry points and trajectories have been proposed. Dandy’s and Keen’s points use more posterior, peritrigonal approaches but are not routinely used because of greater potential for visual pathway injury. Frazier’s occipital–parietal approach is usually recommended for pediatric patients or emergency posterior fossa procedures. The common approach enters frontally at Kocher’s point and aims toward the third ventricle; the authors describe it as quick, straightforward, and having a short learning curve. The patient lies supine with the head neutral and elevated 30–45 degrees to avoid distorting anatomical landmarks. Kocher’s point lies approximately 12 cm from the nasion (1 cm anterior to the coronal suture) and 3 cm lateral from the midline along the midpapillary line. After skin incision, a bur hole and durotomy are made. The catheter is directed toward the medial cantus in the coronal plane and about 1 cm anterior to the tragus in the sagittal plane, then advanced about 7 cm toward the foramen of Monro. Finally, it is tunneled beneath the galea and attached to the external drainage system.

document_sections.heading: 3.6. Complications
document_sections.content: Catheter blockage is among the most frequent EVD complications and requires prompt replacement to prevent acute hydrocephalus. The article associates continuous drainage with a greater incidence of EVD failure, reporting RR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.27–0.74, I-squared = 0%; this statement contrasts with the earlier account of greater catheter obstruction under intermittent drainage. Regardless of management approach, bleeding and catheter misplacement are common, with reported incidence up to 12%. Oral anticoagulants and antiplatelet treatment affect hemorrhagic risk, whereas brain edema and midline shift are the principal reported risks for misplacement. Infection can progress to ventriculitis or cerebritis; its incidence ranges from 0 to 27% and is primarily related to EVD duration. A recent meta-analysis identified continuous drainage as an infection risk factor (RR = 0.20; 95% CI: 0.05–0.72; Isquared = 0%), but found no significant difference between weaning approaches (RR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.06–3.93, I-squared = 73.2%). A 2015 meta-analysis reported an overall infection incidence of 10.6/1000 catheterdays. Its incidence was approximately 19.6/1000 catheter-days when EVD remained for less than 7 days, versus 8/1000 catheter-days when it remained for more than 10 days. A subsequent prospective multicenter cohort from the UK and Ireland reported a 9.3% EVD infection rate at 30 days after placement. In its regression analysis, longer placement procedures and frequent CSF sampling were independently associated with greater ventriculitis risk, regardless of catheter impregnation with antibiotics (i.e., silver). The same study reported that 129 catheters were never sampled and none was associated with catheter infection or ventriculitis.

document_sections.heading: 3.7. External Lumbar Drainage (ELD) for Refractory Intracranial Hypertension in Traumatic Brain Injury
document_sections.content: ELD is used less often for raised ICP after TBI because it might cause iatrogenic transtentorial herniation. It has been used successfully in other settings, including bacterial and cryptococcal meningitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage. The article describes ICP control comparable to ventriculostomy drainage without significant complication rates, but notes that consensus guidelines consider the evidence insufficient to support ELD for ICP control after TBI. Lumbar diversion avoids passing a drain through brain tissue and may be technically and logistically simpler, particularly in isolated TBI with small lateral ventricles that hinder or preclude EVD insertion. Its possible ICP benefit must be weighed against cerebral herniation and associated morbidity and mortality. The authors call for a synthesis comparing its safety and efficacy with EVD to inform practice and research. Abdal-Centallas et al., Levy et al., and Murad et al. reported marked ICP reductions after ELD diversion. All three studies reporting statistical tests found a statistically significant ICP reduction after lumbar drainage. All four studies providing CPP data or observations reported a positive effect, and all four studies describing treatment intensity or other ICP-lowering therapy requirements reported reduced need for other therapies after lumbar drainage. The systematic review data are insufficient for firm conclusions about ELD safety in raised ICP after TBI, although its included studies did not report ELD directly contributing to death. One reported ELD case caused pupillary changes requiring urgent surgery and ended in good neurological recovery; the article also describes this as a case of cerebral herniation requiring surgery. The absence of significant complications in a series of 159 patients with TBI may not resolve reservations about safety. The authors suggest that contemporary clinical and radiological monitoring can permit early recognition of herniation and prompt intervention, despite historical concern about 'coning' after lumbar puncture or drainage. High baseline mortality does not justify potentially harmful treatment. Alternatives generally involve EVD insertion and, if that fails, decompressive craniectomy; neither is low-morbidity. The reported findings, while unreliable for firm inference, suggest a low to very low risk of severe morbidity or mortality from ELD in selected patients. ELD could potentially control ICP without EVD or decompressive craniectomy. Infection occurred at a rate of 3.9% across the included studies, although some infections involved patients with both EVD and ELD. The article compares this with reported ELD infection rates of 4.2–7% and EVD rates of 7-9%.

document_sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
document_sections.content: EVD can save lives in acute hydrocephalus. For SAH, intermittent drainage carries an increased risk of catheter obstruction, hemorrhage, and replacement. The authors conclude that VPS dependency seems higher with RWA than GWA, while the discussion reports differing results across cited studies. In TBI, continuous drainage is conventionally accepted despite the absence of evidence favoring either drainage approach. The benefits of intraventricular thrombolysis in IH/IVH remain under investigation, and randomized trials are needed to define EVD management across clinical settings. The literature appears to support ELD for ICP control after medical treatment has failed, but encouraging safety findings remain insufficient for conclusive recommendations. Its safety and efficacy relative to EVD are unknown, although it appears beneficial for ICP control alone and after EVD failure. Available evidence gives no clear indication that ELD complication rates exceed those of EVD, but cannot establish firm conclusions. Larger prospective observational studies are needed to evaluate an acceptable safety profile, potentially followed by randomized controlled studies assessing therapeutic parity.
